en: Udāna 8.5 Cundasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion, while wandering on tour among the Mallas with a large community of monks, the Blessed One arrived at Pāvā.
There, the Blessed One stayed at Pāvā in Cunda the smith’s mango grove.
Cunda the smith heard: "It is said that the Blessed One, while wandering on tour among the Mallas with a large community of monks, has arrived at Pāvā and is staying at Pāvā in my mango grove."
Then Cunda the smith approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As Cunda the smith was sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma.
Then Cunda the smith, having been instructed, urged, inspired, and gladdened by the Blessed One’s discourse on the Dhamma, said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept my meal for tomorrow, together with the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
The Blessed One consented by remaining silent.
Then Cunda the smith, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.

Then, at the end of that night, Cunda the smith had various kinds of fine food, both hard and soft, prepared in his own residence, including a great quantity of *sūkaramaddava*. He announced the time to the Blessed One, saying:
"It is time, Bhante; the meal is ready.

Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and approached the residence of Cunda the smith together with the community of monks. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed Cunda the smith:
“Cunda, serve me with that *sūkaramaddava* which has been prepared;
as for the other hard and soft foods that have been prepared, serve them to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”

“Yes, venerable sir,” Cunda the smith replied to the Blessed One. He served the Blessed One with the *sūkaramaddava* that had been prepared, and he served the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with the other hard and soft foods that had been prepared.
Then the Blessed One addressed Cunda the smith:
“Cunda, bury that which remains of the *sūkaramaddava* in a pit.

Cunda, I do not see anyone in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, by whom that food, once consumed, could be properly digested, except for the Tathāgata.
“Yes, Bhante,” Cunda the smith replied to the Blessed One. Then he took the remaining *sūkaramaddava*...
Having buried what remained in a pit, Cunda went to the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As Cunda the smith’s son was sitting there, the Blessed One instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened him with a discourse on the Dhamma. Then, rising from his seat, the Blessed One departed.

Then, after the Blessed One had eaten the meal provided by Cunda the smith’s son, a severe illness arose in him. There was a violent attack of dysentery, and piercing pains assailed him, mortal in their intensity.
Yet there, mindful and clearly comprehending, the Blessed One endured them without being disturbed.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come, Ānanda, let us go to Kusinārā.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One.
Having eaten the meal provided by Cunda, [the Blessed One said:]
"Thus have I heard from the blacksmith:
the wise man was afflicted by a severe,
life-ending illness."
And after the Teacher had eaten the sūkaramaddava, a severe illness arose within him;
while being purged, the Blessed One said:
“I am going to the city of Kusinārā.
Then the Blessed One, having stepped down from the road, approached a certain tree root; having approached, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come now, Ānanda, spread out my outer robe folded fourfold; I am weary, Ānanda, and shall sit down.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One and prepared a fourfold robe.
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
Having sat down, the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come now, Ānanda, bring me some water; I am thirsty, Ānanda, I shall drink.
When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Just now, Bhante, about five hundred carts have passed by. That water, churned up by their wheels, flows in small quantities, turbid and muddy.”
“Venerable sir, not far from here is the Kukudhā River, with clear water, pleasant water, cool water, and white water; it has beautiful landing places and is delightful.
There the Blessed One may drink water and cool his limbs.
For a second time... [as before]...
A third time the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Come now, Ānanda, bring me some water; I am thirsty, Ānanda, I shall drink.
“Very well, Bhante,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One, and taking his bowl, he went to where that river was.
Then that river, which had been cut by wheels, shallow, churned, and turbid as it flowed, became clear, serene, and undisturbed as the Venerable Ānanda approached it.
Then this thought occurred to the Venerable Ānanda:
"How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed! Is not the Tathāgata’s great psychic power and great majesty truly extraordinary?"
"For this river, which was previously cut by wheels, shallow, turbulent, and turbid as it flowed, now flows clear, serene, and undisturbed as I approach.
Taking water in his bowl, he approached the Blessed One; having approached, he said this to the Blessed One:
"It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! Such is the great psychic power and the great majesty of the Tathāgata!"
“Venerable sir, this river was previously cut by wheels, shallow, churned up, and turbid as it flowed; yet as I approached it, it flows clear, serene, and undisturbed.
Let the Blessed One drink the water; let the Sugata drink the water.
Then the Blessed One drank the water.
Then the Blessed One, together with a great community of monks, approached the Kukudhā River; having approached,
he plunged into the Kukudhā River, bathed, drank, and having emerged,
he approached a mango grove.
Having approached, he addressed the Venerable Cundaka:
"Come now, Cundaka, spread out my outer robe folded fourfold; I am weary, Cundaka, and wish to lie down.
"Very well, Bhante," the Venerable Cundaka replied to the Blessed One, and having done so, he spread out the outer robe folded fourfold.
Then the Blessed One lay down on his right side in the lion’s posture, placing one foot upon the other, mindful and clearly comprehending, having fixed his mind on the perception of rising.
The Venerable Cundaka, however, sat down right there before the Blessed One.
Having gone to the Kukudha River, the Buddha—
The water was clear, sweet, and serene;
the Teacher, appearing utterly exhausted,
plunged in— this Tathāgata, who is indeed peerless in the world.
Having heard and having drunk, the Teacher crossed over;
preceded by the host of monks in their midst,
the Blessed One, the Teacher, is the one who sets the Dhamma in motion here.
The Great Seer approached the mango grove;
he addressed the bhikkhu named Cundaka:
"Spread out my robe folded fourfold for me to lie upon."
Thus urged by Cunda of purified mind,
he quickly spread out a fourfold-layered rug;
the Teacher, appearing very weary, lay down upon it.
Cunda also sat there at the head [of the group].
Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“It may be, Ānanda, that someone might cause remorse to arise in Cunda the smith’s son:”
“It is a loss for you, friend Cunda; it is a misfortune for you that the Tathāgata, having consumed his last alms-food from you, has attained final Nibbāna.
Ānanda, Cunda the smith’s son should have his remorse dispelled in this way:
“It is a gain for you, friend Cunda; it is a great blessing for you.”
"It was after consuming your final alms-food that the Tathāgata attained final Nibbāna.
Friend Cunda, I have heard this directly from the Blessed One; I have received it directly from him:
'These two alms-meals are equal in fruit, equal in result, and are far more productive of great fruit and great benefit than any other alms-meals.'"
Which two?

That alms-food which, having consumed, the Tathāgata awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; and that alms-food which, having consumed, he attains final nibbāna in the element of nibbāna without residue.
These two alms-meals have equal fruits and equal results; they are far more fruitful and of greater benefit than other alms-meals.
“Kamma conducive to long life has been accumulated by the Venerable Cunda the smith; kamma conducive to beauty has been accumulated by the Venerable Cunda the smith;
kamma conducive to happiness has been accumulated by the Venerable Cunda the smith;
kamma conducive to heaven has been accumulated by the Venerable Cunda the smith.”
“Kamma has been accumulated; kamma leading to fame has been accumulated by the Venerable Cunda the smith;
kamma leading to sovereignty has been accumulated by the Venerable Cunda the smith.
Ānanda, Cunda the smith’s remorse should be dispelled in this way.”
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Merit increases for one who gives;
for one who is self-restrained, enmity does not accumulate.”
The skillful one abandons evil;
through the destruction of lust, hatred, and delusion, he is extinguished.
Thus ends the fifth [verse].
